topic: New GDP Series with Base Year Revised to 2022-23

subtopics.title: Base Year Revision to 2022-23
subtopics.summary: The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation released the New National Accounts Series, with the GDP base year revised from 2011-12 to 2022-23. The 2026 revision is the 8th base year revision since 1948-49 and aligns with System of National Accounts 2008 and the IMF Quarterly National Accounts Manual 2017. A base year is the benchmark for measuring real changes in GDP, CPI and IIP over time. Revisions reflect structural changes in the economy, such as digital services expansion, renewable energy growth and changing consumption patterns.
facts: Released by Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (Rao Inderjit Singh)
New base year is 2022-23; earlier base year was 2011-12
2026 revision is the 8th base year revision since 1948-49
Before 2026, the base year was last updated to 2011-12 in 2015
A base year removes the inflation effect and enables accurate index creation
A base year reflects current economic structure, consumption patterns and price trends
The revision aligns with SNA 2008 and IMF QNA Manual 2017
2022-23 was chosen as the most recent normal economic year after COVID-19 disruptions
Periodic revision follows guidelines of the United Nations Statistical Commission

subtopics.title: Improved Data Sources and Methods
subtopics.summary: The new series integrates high-frequency and administrative datasets, including GST collection, vehicle registration data, PFMS, the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises and the Periodic Labour Force Survey. Double deflation adjusts both output prices and input prices, giving a more accurate measure of real value addition in manufacturing and agriculture. The revision brings the National Pension System and the Old Pension Scheme into government sector accounting. Platform workers, digital economy participants and hired domestic workers are now captured.
facts: GST collection data is one of the new high-frequency and administrative datasets
Vehicle registration data and PFMS are integrated into the new series
Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises and Periodic Labour Force Survey are new data sources
Improves coverage of the informal sector, gig economy, household enterprises and digital activities
Earlier single deflation adjusted only output prices
Double deflation adjusts both output prices and input prices
Double deflation gives more accurate real value addition in manufacturing and agriculture
GDP now includes the National Pension System and the Old Pension Scheme
Captures platform workers, digital economy participants and hired domestic workers

subtopics.title: GDP Concepts and Measurement
subtopics.summary: GDP is the total monetary value of all finished goods and services produced. It can be calculated by three methods: expenditure, production and income. On the expenditure side, GDP equals consumption plus investment plus government expenditure plus exports minus imports. Real GDP is inflation-adjusted GDP, while nominal GDP is GDP at current prices.
facts: GDP is the total monetary value of all finished goods and services produced
Three methods to calculate GDP: expenditure, production and income
Expenditure formula: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M)
C is goods and services consumed; I is investments; G is government expenditures
Real GDP is inflation-adjusted GDP
Nominal GDP is GDP at current prices
GDP at factor cost = GDP at market prices + subsidies - indirect taxes
GDP at market prices is the measure of GDP in India
GDP is not an accurate measure of the overall living standard or well-being of a country
Example: 2021 GDP at current prices Rs 1000; 2022 GDP at current prices Rs 1650; 2022 real GDP at 2021 prices Rs 1100

subtopics.title: Economic Implications of the Revision
subtopics.summary: Real GDP growth is revised upward to 7.6% for FY 2025-26, while nominal GDP is lower at 345.47 lakh crore. Lower nominal GDP can raise the fiscal deficit and debt-to-GDP ratios even though absolute deficit levels are unchanged. Sectoral growth in FY26 is 2.8% in the primary, 9.5% in the secondary and 8.9% in the tertiary sector. More accurate economic data supports policy formulation, investment and business planning.
facts: Real GDP growth revised upward to 7.6% for FY 2025-26
Nominal GDP for FY 2025-26 is 345.47 lakh crore after revision
Fiscal deficit (as % of GDP): revised 4.51%, earlier 4.36%
Debt-to-GDP ratio: revised estimate 57.5% for FY 2026-27, earlier target 55.6%
Lower nominal GDP can raise fiscal deficit and debt-to-GDP ratios despite unchanged absolute deficit levels
Primary sector growth in FY26 is 2.8%, from 5% in FY25
Secondary sector growth in FY26 is 9.5%, from 7.3% in FY25
Tertiary sector growth in FY26 is 8.9%, from 8.3% in FY25
More accurate economic data supports policy formulation, investment and business decisions

quizzes.passage: Gross Domestic Product, or GDP, is the main indicator used to describe the size of an economy. It works as an economic snapshot, helping analysts estimate how much economic activity a country has generated. Statisticians compile the figure within the national accounts framework. Policymakers, investors and businesses use it for planning and investment decisions, so its accuracy matters. The measure relies on a base year, which serves as a benchmark reference point. Using a base year allows economic indicators, price changes and statistical trends to be compared over time. The same reference is used to measure changes in GDP, the consumer price index and the index of industrial production. A base year also helps remove the inflation effect and makes accurate index creation possible. Over time, an economy changes its structure, as digital services expand, renewable energy grows and consumption patterns shift. Periodic revision of the base year is meant to reflect these changes, to follow international guidelines and to improve the accuracy and credibility of GDP estimates. Statistical reforms that update the CPI, IIP and WPI base years are part of a wider effort to modernise India's data system. Such updates aim to strengthen the national framework for economic statistics.

quizzes.passage: Gross Domestic Product is widely used to take a snapshot of an economy and to estimate its growth. At its core, it is the total monetary value of all finished goods and services produced. The figure can be calculated through different approaches, and each approach is one part of how statisticians build the national accounts. Price levels matter when output is compared across years, because a rise in value may reflect higher prices rather than more production. Statisticians therefore rely on a benchmark reference point, known as a base year, to compare economic indicators, price changes and statistical trends. The base year also helps measure changes in indicators that track output and prices, and it removes the inflation effect so that accurate index numbers can be created. Economic structure changes over time, as digital services expand and renewable energy grows. Revising the base year allows the national accounts to reflect these changes. Policymakers, investors and businesses depend on such estimates for planning, which is why accurate data is valued. Improved methodologies and granular data enhance the accuracy of economic growth estimates, and a revised framework better captures the digital economy and platform-based work. Statistical reforms update the consumer price index, the index of industrial production and the wholesale price index base years.

quizzes.passage: The New National Accounts Series was released by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, with the base year for Gross Domestic Product revised to 2022-23. The new series uses improved estimation methods and aligns with the System of National Accounts 2008. It integrates high-frequency and administrative datasets, including GST collections, vehicle registration data and the Periodic Labour Force Survey. The base year 2022-23 was chosen because it represents the most recent normal economic year after the COVID-19 disruptions. The revision also changes how government finances are estimated, and the national accounts now capture more platform workers and hired domestic workers than before. Headline figures for the year 2025-26 are presented afresh under the new base year. The revision seeks to improve the accuracy and credibility of the national accounts. The new series also reflects the digital economy and new sectors more closely, so that the measured economy reflects present production structures. Improved methodologies and granular data enhance the accuracy of the economic growth rate. Statistical reforms modernise India's data system through updated CPI, IIP and WPI base years, strengthening the national framework. The Periodic revision of the base year follows guidelines of the United Nations Statistical Commission. The series covers gig work and household enterprises as well.

quizzes.passage: A revision of the national accounts can change many figures at once. Once the base year is updated, the estimates for recent years are recalculated, so the size of the economy and its growth path both shift. The new series for the year 2025-26 is released with a revised base, and the change affects how the economy looks compared with earlier estimates. The economy has changed in structure, with digital services expansion, renewable energy growth and changing consumption patterns. A periodic revision is meant to reflect these shifts in the data. The new series also integrates high-frequency datasets, including GST collections and vehicle registration data, which add to the coverage of the informal sector, gig economy and household enterprise activity. Government sector accounting has been improved, and the estimates of government finances are now more accurate. Better economic data is expected to help policy formulation, investment and business planning. The revision is therefore presented as an improvement in statistical reliability for the country. Improved methodologies and granular data enhance the accuracy of the economic growth rate. The base year 2022-23 was chosen as the most recent normal economic year after the COVID-19 disruptions. The series is aligned with the System of National Accounts 2008.
